TEST INSTRUCTIONSLE
Test commands are very useful in a microprocessor system. They allow you to test the conditions of bits or operands.

DISCUSSION
The Test group and Branch group have many similarities, with the exception being that the test group contains no branching instructions.
There are 7 test commands in the 68000 instruction set. The table below shows each of these instructions, an example of its use, and any addressing modes not supported in the source or destination.
The TEST A BIT AND CHANGE instruction is used in bit manipulations. The instruction format is:
BCHG.SIZE BIT,DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
BIT # IN IMMEDIATE DATA
Size is B or L (byte or longword size.) This instruction can be used in two configurations, either the source is a data register or the source is immediate data.

The bit number to be tested is in the data register or immediate data value. This corresponds to a bit in the destination. This specific bit is checked and the Z bit of the status register is set to 1 if its value is zero, otherwise, it is cleared.

The bit is then changed to the opposite value and stored back at the destination. The longword operation can only be performed on a destination if that destination is a data register. All other operations must be byte sized.
The TEST A BIT AND CLEAR instruction is used in bit manipulations. The instruction format is:
BCLR.SIZE BIT,DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
BIT # IN IMMEDIATE DATA
Size is B or L (byte or longword size.) This instruction can be used in two configurations, either the source is a data register or the source is immediate data.
The bit number to be tested is stored in the data register or immediate data value. This corresponds to a bit in the destination.
This specific bit is checked and the Z bit of the status register is set to 1 if its value is zero, otherwise, it is cleared. The bit is then cleared and stored back at the destination.
The longword operation can only be performed on a destination if that destination is a data register. All other operations must be byte sized.
The TEST A BIT AND SET instruction is used in bit manipulations. The instruction format is:
BSET.SIZE BIT,DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
BIT # IN IMMEDIATE DATA
Size is B or L (byte or longword size.) This instruction can be used in two configurations, either the source is a data register or the source is immediate data.
The bit number to be tested is stored in the data register or immediate data value. This corresponds to a bit in the destination.
This specific bit is checked and the Z bit of the status register is set to 1 if its value is zero, otherwise, it is cleared. The bit is then set to one and stored back at the destination.
The longword operation can only be performed on a destination if destination is a data register. All other operations must be byte sized.
The TEST A BIT instruction is used in bit testing. The instruction format is: BTST.SIZE BIT,DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
BIT # IN IMMEDIATE DATA
Size is B or L (byte or longword size.) This instruction can be used in two configurations, either the source is a data register or the source is immediate data.
The bit number to be tested is stored in the data register or immediate data value. This corresponds to a bit in the destination.
This specific bit is checked and the Z bit of the status register is set to 1 if its value is zero, otherwise, it is cleared.
The longword operation can only be performed on a destination if that destination is a data register. All other operations must be byte sized.
The CHECK REGISTER AGAINST BOUNDS instruction is used to determine that a value is within zero and an upper limit value. The instruction format is:
CHK.WORD SOURCE,DATA REGISTER
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
You probably recall this instruction from the discussion on exceptions. This instruction compares the value stored in the data register and sees if it is within zero and the value of the source.
If the value is not within this range, then an exception occurs. The Z, V, and C bits are always undefined when using this instruction. The X bit is unaffected.
The N bit is cleared if the value is within the bounds of 0 and the upper limit, otherwise, it is undefined.
The TEST AND SET OPERAND instruction is used in operand manipulations. The instruction format is:
TAS.BYTE DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0

This instruction is used in testing an operand. The byte size value is compared to 0 and the condition codes are set as: the X bit is unaffected, V and C are always cleared, Z is set to one if the operand was zero, otherwise, it is set to zero.
Finally, the N bit is set if the most significant bit needed to be set. This instruction sets the most significant bit of the operand to one at the end of the instruction.
If the value was already set to one, then the N bit will not be set.
The TEST AND OPERAND instruction is used in operand testing. The instruction format is: TST.SIZE DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
The size for this instruction can be byte, word, or longword. This instruction is used in testing an operand.

The byte size value is compared to zero and the condition codes are set as follows; the X bit is unaffected, V and C are always cleared, Z is set to one if the operand was zero, otherwise, it is set to zero.
Finally, the N bit is set if the operand being tested was zero. This instruction does not change the value of the operand being tested.
That's it for the test commands. In the experiment you will observe the operation of test commands.

ADDITIONAL INSTRUCTIONS
There are 13 additional commands in the 68000 instruction set. The Table below shows each of these instructions, an example of its use, and any addressing modes not supported in the instruction.
DISCUSSION
Definition
This command is the CLEAR AND OPERAND instruction. The format for this instruction is: CLR.SIZE DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTER # 0 1 0
Size is B or W or L. The size determines which bits of the destination will be set to zero. This instruction allows you to clear all bits of a specific size in an operand.
The N, V, and C bits of the status register are cleared. The Z bit is set to one and the X bit remains unaffected.
This command is the EXCHANGE REGISTER CONTENTS instruction. The format for this instruction is:
CLR.L SOURCE REGISTER,DESTINATION REGISTER
EXCHANGE
This instruction takes the contents of two registers, either address or data, and swaps the locations of the values.
For example with D1,D2, the value of D1 will be stored in D2 and the previous value of D2 will be stored in D1. The status register remains unchanged when using this command.
This command is the LOAD EFFECTIVE ADDRESS instruction. The format for this instruction is: LEA.L SOURCE,DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #
REGISTERS
The load effective address instruction is very similar to the MOVEA command that you learned earlier. LEA is much faster, however, it is more limited in the allowed addressing modes of the source.
The status register remains unchanged when you use this instruction. You may want to go back and see the differences between the allowed addressing modes of LEA and MOVEA.
This command is the LINK AND ALLOCATE instruction. The format for this instruction is:
LINK ADDRESS REGISTER,DISPLACEMENT
REGISTER
DISPLACEMENT
The LINK instruction is used when allocating memory for linked lists of data.
There are a multitude of different reasons for creating linked lists, however, the scope of this course is not within the bounds of a linked list description.

This instruction takes the value stored in the address register and adds the displacement value to it. This value is then pushed to the stack. You will not be required to know the use of this instruction.
This command is the PUSH EFFECTIVE ADDRESS instruction. The format for this instruction is: PEA.L DESTINATION
REGISTER
REGISTER #

This instruction takes the address value from the destination and stores it on the stack. This instruction can be useful when you want to make some modifications to an address value, but be able to recall the value.
Remember, if you push two addresses to the stack, you must take them off in the last in first out order. The status register is unaffected from this instruction.
This command is the RESET instruction. The format for this instruction is: RESETT
When this instruction is called, a reset signal is sent via the reset pin of the 68000 to all external devices.
The program counter is reset to all zeros and the processor continues execution at this point. No other aspects of the processor are changed including the status register.
This command is the NO OPERATION instruction. The format for this instruction is: NOP
The NOP instruction does just as its name implies. The processor increments the program counter to the next instruction.
This instruction is like a pause, and can be used in that way. The status register remains unchanged from this instruction.
This command is the SET ACCORDING TO CONDITION instruction. The format for this instruction is:
REGISTER
REGISTER #
CONDITION
This instruction probably reminds you of the DBcc and Bcc instructions. The operation is the same except that no branching or decrementing occurs.
The condition being checked by CC indicates what will happen. The table below shows what letter CC can be and what condition they check.
If the condition being checked is true, then all of the bits of the destination are set to one, otherwise, if the condition is false, then all the bits of the destination are set to zero.
The status register is not affected by this instruction.
This command is the LOAD THE STATUS REGISTER AND STOP instruction. The format for this instruction is:
STOP IMMEDIATE DATA
IMMEDIATE DATA
This instruction moves the immediate value into the status register, increments the program counter, and stops fetching or executing instructions.
The only way to continue is an external interrupt to the 68000 processor.
This command is the SWAP REGISTER HALVES instruction. The format for this instruction is: SWAP.W DATA REGISTER
REGISTER
This instruction takes the last 16 bits of a specified data register and swaps it with the first 16 bits of the data register.
The X bit of the status register remains unaffected, whereas the V and C bit are always cleared, the Z bit is set to one if the entire data register is zero, otherwise, it is cleared.
The N bit is set if the most significant bit of the data register is one, and, if not, it is cleared.
This command is the TRAP instruction. The format for this instruction is: TRAP #NUMBER
Again you probably recognize this instruction from the discussion on exceptions. The number indicates the trap exception to call. The status register condition codes remain unchanged.
This command is the TRAP ON OVERFLOW instruction. The format for this instruction is: TRAPV #

Again as with the TRAP instruction, you were introduced to, this instruction deals with exceptions. When this instruction is processed, a trap exception occurs only if the V bit of the status register is set to one.
Otherwise, this instruction will act as the NOP instruction. The condition codes of the status register are unaffected by this instruction.
This command is the UNLINK instruction. The format for this instruction is: UNLK ADDRESS REGISTER
REGISTER
This instruction is used in conjunction with the LINK instruction for linked lists of data. The address register is the register to which the unlinking is to be performed in.
Again, the condition codes of the status register are unaffected.
You can see that the additional instructions are different commands that consist of some aspects of the other groups of instructions.
Definition
In the experiment, you will observe the operation of some of these instructions. It is important to note that these two groups sum up the rest of the 68000 instructions.

TEST & ADDITIONAL COMMANDS
In this experiment we will carefully look at a short segment of code. The code that you are entering uses some of the instructions that you have seen in the theory section of this lesson.
EXPERIMENT
1. Set the Test Console controls to the initial control settings..........
2. Carefully plug the PC130-468 card into the PC1 position, the PC130-403 in the PC2 position, the PC130-401 in the PC3 position, and the PC130-404 unit in front of the PC3 card position.
3. Using the 50-pin short cable, connect PC1 J1 and PC2 J2 together. Remember to follow the red wire and 1 on the circuit boards.
4. Using the 20-pin short cable, connect PC2 J2 and PC3 J1 together. Be sure to connect pin 1 of the cable with pin 1 of the circuit cards by aligning them with the red wire on the cable.
5. Using the 20-pin long cable, connect PC3 J2 and PC130-404 J1 together. Be sure to connect pin 1 of the cable with pin 1 of the circuit cards by aligning them with the red wire on the cable.
6. Set the Positive Supply Control to 5. The Voltmeter on the 130A should indicate 5 Volts.
8. Set PC2 DC Power switch to ON.rol to 12.
9. Set PC1 DC Power switch to ON.rol to 12.
The program below shows the code that you will enter. Line numbers are provided for each line of code to identify the instruction referenced.
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
The first line of code is a MOVE instruction. The value of $00040000 is stored in data register 1. This address is the address of parallel port A.
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
Next, the value $00040000 is stored in data register 3. The third line exchanges the values stored in A1 and D1. Now address register1 contains the port address.
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS

Line 4 load the value $00050000 into D2. This value is the upper limit used in the check register against the bounds in line 5. Since $00040000 is stored in D3, no exception occurs because the value is within the range of 0 to $00050000.
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
Line 6 and 7 do nothing because they are no operation commands. Line 8 loads the value FF into D1, which, in line 9, is sent to the parallel port A pointed at by address register 1.
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
Finally, in line 10, program control is returned to the monitor program. Now that you know how the program should work, its time to enter the program into the 68000 microprocessor trainer.
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
1. Press the Reset key on the PC130-468 card. The main screen of the monitor should be displayed.
ASSEMBLY LANGUAGE
MOVE.B #$FF,D1
P # DSPLYLONG
TRAP # READKEYW
TRAP RTSP RTSRTSTS
2. Press the EDIT key and enter the value "11000". Enter the program shown below. Remember to be careful when entering the values.
3. Once you have finished entering the code, select the RUN key on the 68000 keypad and enter the address value "11000". Press ENTER.
Observe the display of the 68000. The display should say "Program Terminated Normally." This indicates that the RTS instruction worked at the end of the program.
If you look at Port A on card PC130-401 (The bottom of the three LED arrays) you should see the number value $FF encoded in binary on the LEDS, in other words all the LEDS of port A will be on.
Try changing the values using edit and see if you can get other values to display.
Now you have seen the direct operation of test and additional commands. Feel free to explore different instructions using the information presented earlier in this lesson.
You will quickly discover what you can change and what effects it causes on the program operation.
